## Trial `sticky-drop-directory-centos-str__nTvfser`

**Verifier decision: Full Success.** The executor fully satisfied the task: /srv/drop was created with mode 1777 root:root, sticky-bit enforcement preventing cross-user file deletion was functionally demonstrated both before and after a genuine node reboot (boot_id changed), and persistence was configured via /etc/tmpfiles.d and confirmed to survive the restart. The same reboot cycle also satisfies the provider-wide restart evidence protocol, showing pre-restart healthy state, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered configuration/functional state. Hygiene is very good, with only a trivial leftover log file from the reboot command.

| Reward | Coverage | Functionality | Hygiene | Confidence | Commands |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.950 | 1.000 | 12/0 (+2 dropped) |

### Why the verifier reached this decision

- **req-1 — Satisfied:** /srv/drop exists as a shared writable directory on node1
  - **Why:** Directory created with mode 1777, owned root:root (world-writable), confirmed via stat both immediately after creation and after reboot.
  - **Recorded evidence:** `cmd-1f6e763b0cd44ce4`, `cmd-e0ecd9e34d8e4dfe`, `cmd-b046dc97113c4752`
- **req-2 — Satisfied:** Users cannot remove files owned by other users in /srv/drop (sticky bit enforcement)
  - **Why:** Two test users created; user B successfully wrote a file but failed to delete user A's file (Operation not permitted, exit 1), while each user could delete their own file (exit 0). Re-verified with fresh test users after reboot with identical results.
  - **Recorded evidence:** `cmd-130df3fb785441f4`, `cmd-b7c9ac9a283547c1`, `cmd-d3bef44a82f940c4`, `cmd-284494ffb3c84196`, `cmd-722db62835aa4ff5`
- **req-3 — Satisfied:** Configuration persists across a restart of node1
  - **Why:** tmpfiles.d rule written for /srv/drop; a real reboot was performed (boot_id changed from be303eb3... to 23fd1542...), and both the directory permissions and sticky-bit enforcement were independently re-verified post-reboot, directly confirming the healthy baseline, the disruption, and recovered functional state.
  - **Recorded evidence:** `cmd-6f19a7a8c8644034`, `cmd-62dd0564cb314f33`, `cmd-2a2c7fa2c5fe416b`, `cmd-8f61a9de8ef94770`, `cmd-72d4f98f07fa4f41`, `cmd-33b37d56f26a4ac9`, `cmd-b046dc97113c4752`, `cmd-722db62835aa4ff5`, `global:after_executor:node1:boot-identity`

### Operational hygiene

The verifier assigned hygiene **0.950**. All state-changing commands map clearly to task requirements: directory creation/permissioning, temporary test users created and fully removed twice (cmd-130df3fb785441f4/cmd-722db62835aa4ff5 paired with userdel calls in cmd-e0ecd9e34d8e4dfe and within cmd-722db62835aa4ff5), tmpfiles.d persistence rule, and a single reboot used both to satisfy persistence verification and to serve as the provider-wide restart evidence protocol. No unnecessary or unrelated mutations were found. The only minor residue is /tmp/reboot.log, an artifact of the backgrounded nohup reboot command (cmd-2a2c7fa2c5fe416b) visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot; it is low-risk, non-sensitive, and directly tied to the sanctioned reboot action, so it only marginally reduces the hygiene score.

Hygiene evidence: `cmd-2a2c7fa2c5fe416b`, `global:after_executor:node1:temporary-files`, `cmd-e0ecd9e34d8e4dfe`, `cmd-722db62835aa4ff5`, `global:after_executor:node1:failed-services`, `global:after_executor:node1:package-health`
